name: Food combining diet

card.summary: A way of eating that separates proteins, starches and fruit across meals, which followers use hoping for leaner weight, better digestion and a clearer, less bloated look.
card.note: The one randomised trial found weight loss similar to a balanced diet with the same calories.

quick.overview:
Food combining is a set of eating rules that keep certain foods apart: proteins away from starches, fruit eaten alone, and so on. Followers use it to aim for a leaner body, less bloating and better skin and energy, which feed into how they look.

The best-known version is the Hay Diet from the early twentieth century. A 2000 randomised trial in 54 obese patients found that a food-combining diet and a balanced diet with the same calories produced similar weight loss and metabolic changes.
quick.how: Practitioners plan meals so that a protein is paired with non-starchy vegetables, a starch with vegetables, and fruit is eaten alone or before a meal. Some versions also restrict dairy and cold drinks at meals. Followers often report changes in bloating within days.
quick.risks: The diet is generally a restriction of meal composition rather than of food groups, so risks are mainly practical, such as complicated meal planning. Rigid food rules can be hard to sustain, and people with medical conditions or a history of disordered eating are usually advised to consult a clinician before adopting restrictive patterns.

lead: Food combining, also called trophology, is a dietary approach built on rules about which foods may be eaten together at one meal. The usual rules keep concentrated proteins and starches apart, eat fruit alone or before meals, and pair vegetables with either group.[1][2] People adopt it to manage weight, reduce bloating and improve digestion, which they associate with a leaner midsection, clearer skin and a better-looking body.

The best-known form is the Hay Diet, named after the New York physician William Howard Hay, and the approach was further spread in the mid-twentieth century by the naturopath Herbert M. Shelton in Food Combining Made Easy (1951).[1][2] Ayurvedic texts also contain a concept of incompatible food pairings, which writers sometimes cite as an older parallel.[2]

Research is limited. A 2000 randomised trial compared a food-combining diet to a balanced diet at equal energy intake and found similar weight and metabolic changes in both groups.[3] Nutrition writers describe the underlying digestive claims as not supported by physiology, and followers' reports of benefits are mostly anecdotal.

chain: Meals planned around separated food groups
Often reduces calories and processed food as a side effect
angle.text: Followers use food combining as a structured way to plan meals, aiming for weight loss, less bloating and a leaner look. The trial that exists found its weight loss matched that of a balanced diet with the same calories.

infobox: William Howard Hay; Herbert M. Shelton
Separate starches and proteins; eat fruit alone

paras: Food combining holds that different food types need different digestive conditions, so mixing them is said to cause fermentation, bloating or poor nutrient use. Typical rules include not combining protein with starch, eating fruit on an empty stomach, and drinking little or no cold water with meals.[1][2]

Hay's system sorted foods into acid-forming, alkaline-forming and neutral groups and recommended that meals centre on one category with vegetables.[2] Later popular versions, such as Doris Grant and Jean Joice's Food Combining for Health (1984), adapted the rules for weight loss.[2]

Wikipedia notes that Edgar Cayce discussed the idea earlier and that Shelton popularised it in 1951; the Hay Diet is the version most often cited, and Hay reported losing weight on it.[1] Grokipedia traces the theme further back to Ayurvedic concepts of incompatible foods and to nineteenth-century hygiene movements.[2] More recently, social-media wellness influencers have promoted paid food-combining programmes.[1]

Proponents say that separating foods eases digestion, boosts energy and supports weight management.[2] Within appearance-focused communities, the same idea is used in the hope of reducing bloating and water retention for a leaner look.

Reviewers describe the central digestive claims as unsupported, noting that the stomach and intestine handle mixed meals through overlapping enzyme activity.[1][2] Wikipedia describes the diet as a fad diet promoted largely through testimonials.[1]

A randomised in-hospital trial assigned 54 obese patients to a 1,100 kcal food-combining diet or a balanced diet with equal energy for six weeks. Weight loss was 6.2 kg and 7.5 kg respectively, with no significant difference, and both groups saw similar falls in body fat, waist-to-hip ratio, glucose, insulin and lipids.[3] No other controlled human trials of food combining are known.

timeline.event: William Howard Hay develops his acid-alkaline separation approach; Health via Food appears in 1929.[2]
Herbert M. Shelton publishes Food Combining Made Easy.[1]
Doris Grant and Jean Joice publish Food Combining for Health.[2]
Randomised trial compares food combining with a balanced diet.[3]
